title: Agent Permissions Best Practices
summary: Six practices for sizing an agent's access, with the real scope names, the vendor limits, the token shape decision, and what revoking a grant actually does at Google, Microsoft, Slack and GitHub.
body_markdown:
TL;DR


**The permission that causes the incident is rarely the one anyone approved on purpose. It is the one nobody took back.**


The providers have already conceded the point in their own defaults. Microsoft calls application permissions "highly privileged" and says the delegated model "is the recommended approach whenever it meets the application's requirements." Google requires that an app "that only reads data must not request access to read, write, and delete content when a more narrow scope is available." GitHub now tells you outright to stop using classic tokens.


The common instinct is that granting broadly is efficient, because enumerating actions is slow and a broad role works on the first try. It is efficient exactly once. Every capability an agent holds but does not use is still in its blast radius the day a prompt gets manipulated or a tool call goes wrong.


We are not arguing for a review board on every scope. Most of this is mechanical: pick the token shape that carries the user, name the action rather than the system, and let a scheduled review delete what nobody can justify.


Start with the agent nobody has looked at since it shipped, and read its granted scopes against the provider's own least-privileged recommendation for each call it makes.
